rewrites.summary:
Kazakhstan demands real caution from trans visitors — Central Asia's most liveable country for trans people, a relative statement within its region. Nothing is criminalised: no propaganda statute, no bathroom law, and no police targeting pattern — police are unhelpful rather than predatory. Legal gender recognition exists but is heavily medicalised (psychiatric boards, surgery requirements applied in practice). An international monitoring body recorded 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents in 2024 — real incidents, yet documented and reported, which itself signals a functioning civil society (Feminita, ECOM).

For a visitor: no legal exposure; low visibility keeps visitor exposure small; the main cities are navigable.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Trajectory and regional flux: a petition against open and hidden propaganda gained official review by the Ministry of Culture in 2024, a step a human-rights organisation urged the government to reject, and anti-gender MPs are vocal — a live direction-of-travel signal with no statute enacted yet. Since 2022 hundreds of trans people have fled to Kazakhstan from neighbouring Russia after Russia's propaganda law and ban on legal gender recognition — the country reads as a refuge by comparison, not a destination that is safe in itself.
rewrites.localsOnly: The heavily medicalised legal-gender-recognition process is resident-facing: psychiatric boards and surgery requirements are applied in practice to residents, not to visitors.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The propaganda petition remains under official review as of the 2024 reports; whether it ripens into a statute is unresolved. The police-are-unhelpful description rests on behavioural reporting that could not be independently verified. The ECOM regional report is abstract-level, with country data held in a linked report body.

An international monitoring body's hate-crime reporting summary for this country: it has not reported hate-crime data since the 2018 report, has no nominated point of contact for hate crimes, and would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures — an institutional-gap finding on documentation of bias violence.

Blind mirrors drop region name, city names, org names and the invent-orgs; seat-of-culture genericised (ministry, international monitoring body).

rewrites.summary: Nicaragua is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans — sodomy was decriminalised in 2008 — but NGOs document 108 cases of violence against the LGBTIQ+ community in 2024 alone and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years, and arbitrary detention is used broadly against perceived opponents. Since 2018 virtually all independent civil society has been shut down or exiled, so there is no domestic protection infrastructure and no recourse for a visitor facing harm.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The broader regime context colours the visit: the crackdown that began after the 2018 protests left at least 325 dead and more than 2,000 injured per the regional human-rights commission, and the official climate is one of impunity — an assessment documents a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived regime enemies that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, with anti-LGBTI abuse listed among significant violations.
rewrites.localsOnly: The documented violence falls on residents: 108 cases of violence against the LGBTIQ+ community in 2024 and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years. The civil-society shutdown affects resident organisations and the residents who depended on them.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The violence and murder totals are NGO-counted resident tallies; how far visitors appear in them is unresolved. Generalised repression is regime-wide, so detention risk is not trans-specific; conversely the trans-murder count is trans-specific and cannot be generalised to visitors.

A national government's annual human-rights reporting on this country: documents a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived regime enemies that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among significant violations — an official assessment that anti-LGBTI abuse occurs inside a climate of impunity.

An international rights organisation (May 2019): the post-2018 crackdown left at least 325 dead and more than 2,000 injured per the regional human-rights commission; a journalist describes being beaten by a pro-government mob and targeted partly for being gay, documenting homophobia within the repression, with the casualty figures.

News reporting (Nov 2007): a new penal code, effective March 2008, repealed the 1992 sodomy law (1–3 years' imprisonment), whose vague wording had also been usable against LGBT-rights campaigning and sexual-health work — dated decriminalisation: same-sex conduct not criminalised since 2008.

Blind drops all proper names and the regime figure's name; numbers preserved.

rewrites.summary:
Suriname is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors — legally unremarkable, socially mixed. Same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's 'any other status' clause is read to cover SOGI discrimination, and the penal code has carried sexual-orientation discrimination and hate-speech provisions since March 2015. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-murder pattern, but the capital's small community reports routine harassment, and the interior has essentially no protection.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest street risk in the capital; low tourist infrastructure generally.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Institutional and litigation flux: the authorities told UN rights bodies their laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, while experts pressed on implementing a regional court's judgment on transgender identity — implementation status remains in motion. Civil-society groups also report being excluded from official consultative processes despite repeated requests.
rewrites.localsOnly: No legal gender recognition — a resident-facing gap. The 2022 Equal Treatment Labour Act adds employment protections for workers, and the harassment reports concern residents' daily street experience; the community also reports continued daily discrimination despite the constitutional reading.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The absence of any documented trans-murder pattern is an absence-of-evidence finding, not proof of safety. Interior protection levels and the real-world operation of the 2022 labour act are unverified. Community harassment reports are anecdotal rather than systematically counted.

blindSourceSummaries: A regional rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal for men and women nationwide; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations CAN register; a constitution clause of 'any other status' is read by the authorities as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity despite no explicit statutory protection.

A civil-society report (July 2024): the constitution covers SOGI only implicitly through 'any other status', and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since 1869; the report urges a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

A national government's annual human-rights reporting (2015) for this country: documents a former leader's trial, police brutality, corruption, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex (LGBTI) persons and other minorities'.

A submission to a UN human-rights body from local groups and partners: despite constitutional protection, LGBTI persons still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation; in March 2015 a penal code was revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation.

A UN human-rights committee review of this country (July 2024): the authorities asserted their laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, backed by a national inclusive labour-market commission, while experts pressed on implementing a regional human-rights court's judgment on transgender identity; the review welcomed the abolition of the death penalty in the penal code (2015) and military code (2021).

A UN pre-review summary (March 2016) from the local platform: since a 2011 review the country revised its penal code to equalise the age of consent for same- and opposite-sex conduct and to add sexual-orientation discrimination provisions; the platform also reports exclusion from official consultative processes despite repeated requests.
rewrites.notes: Split per rule 6: visitor assessment (decriminalisation, SOGI-reading, penal-code provisions, street risk) in summary; UN-review/inter-state implementation flux in tangentialFactors; LGR absence, labour act, harassment and inclusion complaints as resident-facing in localsOnly (per current_localsOnly); lack-of-evidence and unverified-operation caveats in outOfScopeNotes. Blind genericises institutions (UN bodies, regional courts) and drops city/org names.

rewrites.summary:
Kyrgyzstan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has been legal since 1998 and there is no expression statute, but legal gender recognition has been removed, police abuse and extortion of LGBT people are documented, and an active anti-LGBT political campaign is running in the country — in 2023-2024 two discriminatory laws targeted the LGBTI community and restricted LGBTI organisations, with homophobic and transphobic legislator rhetoric accompanying them.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but LGR removal, a police extortion culture, and the political campaign make being outed risky.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The trajectory is sharply negative: once the region's relative haven and a liberal beacon, the country is now regressing, and the contraction of public LGBT life is documented — the capital's lone LGBT club closed in 2017 in an atmosphere tied by reporting to a ban on 'LGBT propaganda', and no other venue remained.
rewrites.localsOnly: The 2020 law blocking birth-certificate changes removed legal gender recognition — a resident-facing status. The NGO-restriction laws of 2023-2024 affect resident organisations, and the resident community operates under pressure, with stigma from law enforcement documented.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The record says there is no expression statute, but source reporting ties the capital's LGBT-club closures to a ban on 'LGBT propaganda' — the two cannot be reconciled from the material here. Whether the 2023-2024 discriminatory laws are actively enforced is not documented. One monitoring body dates LGR removal to 2021 while the civil-status amendment blocking birth-certificate changes dates to 2020 — the discrepancy is unresolved.

A trans-rights index (2024): this country (2021) is among the units that removed the right to legal gender recognition; for this country and several neighbours the 'bare minimum' of not banning recognition is all they score — the regional floor on trans legal status.

A rights organisation's country profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): consensual same-sex activity decriminalised in 1998 with age of consent equal at 16; no same-sex marriage or civil unions, and a 2016 constitutional amendment explicitly bans same-sex marriage; the provision allowing trans people to change legal gender markers was removed by a 2020 amendment to the law on civil status.
A regional study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention and hormone treatment across the region — includes information for trans migrants.

News reporting (19 Oct 2017): why the capital's only gay club closed — the capital had been a relatively safe haven and liberal beacon until a ban on 'LGBT propaganda'; the feature documents the closing of organised gay nightlife.

Blind drops the community org name, city names and monitoring organisations; keeps law/date facts.

rewrites.summary:
Tajikistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation in the country shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids, registry practices, and zero recourse make discovery dangerous.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The wider environment is one of hardening repression: a 2017 world report chronicled opposition leaders sentenced and human-rights lawyers imprisoned in 2016, and the community is described as one of the most closed in society. The 2022 anti-discrimination law is assessed as failing to address discrimination, so written protection does not translate into practice.
rewrites.localsOnly: The informal registries of LGBT residents and the on-paper medicalised legal-gender-recognition route are resident-facing, and the raid pattern primarily targets residents — police have used fake meetings to register people in a database, harvested social-media contacts, and used forced or sham marriages against LGBT people with police inaction.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the on-paper medicalised registration route is ever granted in practice is unverified. Registry practices are maintained informally, so their current status is opaque. The 2022 anti-discrimination law is on the books but assessed as failing to address discrimination — a gap between statute and practice.

A rights organisation's overview (updated Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal throughout the country since independence, no SOGI non-discrimination protection; in 2024 a regional programme recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people with police arbitrary arrests, blackmail and extortion; a 2017 government registry of 'proven' LGBT persons was flagged — legality without safety.

A regional study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention and hormone treatment across the region — maps what gender-affirming and HIV care is actually reachable in-country and includes guidance for trans migrants.

A regional rights-monitoring annual review 2025: police lure LGBT people into fake meetings to register them in a database, harvest social-media contacts and extort money (10+ cases in one region); forced or sham marriages used against LGBT people with police inaction; the 2022 anti-discrimination law only partially aligns with international standards.

A regional legislative analysis (2020): comparative analysis identifying legal barriers and gaps for gay men and trans people, built from a questionnaire completed by local partners — documents where the written law protects but practice does not.

A world report (2017) chapter: the human-rights situation deteriorated sharply in 2016 — opposition leadership sentenced, human-rights lawyers imprisoned, and a predetermined referendum extending presidential rule — the repressive context surrounding LGBT life.

News commentary (Jan 2013): despite decriminalisation 15 years earlier (1998) there is very little tolerance; those who disclose orientation become targets of physical and psychological abuse including from police, and the community remains one of the most closed in society — social-climate evidence predating the 2016 registry.
rewrites.notes: Split per rule 6: raids and enforcement risk in summary (visitor discovery danger); repressive-context and anti-discrimination-law gap in tangentialFactors; registries, on-paper LGR and forced-marriage practice as resident-facing in localsOnly (per current_localsOnly); on-paper route verification and registry opacity in outOfScopeNotes. Blind genericises organisations (rights organisation, regional programme, world report) and drops city/region names.

rewrites.summary: Laos demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans in this country, which has a socially visible tradition of trans-feminine people; but there is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, no registered LGBT organisation — the one-party system restricts all civil society — and no documented recourse. The tourist cities are accustomed to tourists; the risk is administrative (an opaque system) more than violent.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The permissive legal baseline is itself a historic inheritance: same-sex conduct has never been formally criminalised, with a penal code modelled on the historic administration, and the online space is tightening — LGBT expression operates under official attention, though diplomatic visibility exists: an international day against homophobia and transphobia was marked in the capital.
rewrites.localsOnly: No legal gender recognition and no registered LGBT organisations are resident-facing gaps: the one-party system restricts all civil society, so resident organisations cannot register.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Civil-society restrictions affect all, not visitors specifically; no trans-specific enforcement mechanism is documented anywhere in the record. One diplomatic source page could not be fully retrieved, so its detail rests on its summary.

A first-person account (2000): during a week in the capital the writer met a small circle of lesbians and gay men whose lives centred on a few restaurants and friendship networks — the scene is small, discreet and social rather than public or institutional.

News in-depth (Oct 2018): government crackdown on social media — influential users (internet celebrities) face retribution for posts, and the country's only LGBT advocacy group is quoted — online LGBT expression operating under tightening official attention.

Blind drops country/city names and the advocacy-group name; keeps institutional genericisation.

rewrites.summary:
Timor-Leste is workable for trans visitors — a country where same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's equality provisions have been read inclusively, and the capital hosts an annual Pride march with government participation, remarkable for a young, Catholic-majority nation. There is no legal gender recognition and services are thin, but no pattern of police targeting or anti-trans violence is documented, and the small community operates openly.

For a visitor: no documented risk pattern; the constraint is thin services and the absence of legal gender recognition rather than active hostility.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: A regional leadership comparison colours the visit: while neighbouring countries turn hostile, the capital's Pride events have grown — the first march in 2017, again in 2018, and a 2019 parade estimated at 3,000 people, six times the first turnout, with the country's leader publicly backing the event. Reporting also captures day-to-day rejection alongside the headline acceptance, such as a lead organiser's own family's hostile messages.
rewrites.localsOnly: Service thinness and the absence of legal gender recognition are resident-facing gaps; the small community (CODIVA, Arco Iris) operates openly.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The absence of a documented police-targeting or anti-trans-violence pattern is an absence-of-evidence finding, not proof of safety. Service thinness is unquantified. Participation and endorsement claims rest on news reporting. The Catholic-majority character is a social qualifier, not a legal fact.

blindSourceSummaries: A volunteer-programme guide: same-sex sexual acts decriminalised in 1975; an international human-rights joint statement on SOGI was adopted in 2011; the country voted in favour of a 2013 international resolution on vulnerability and disability — the legal and policy context for living openly.

News feature (June 2018): the first-ever Pride parade in 2017 drew international attention and a televised endorsement from the prime minister, while the report also captures day-to-day rejection (the organiser's family's messages) — social-climate depth beyond the headline acceptance.

News reporting (July 2018): the second annual LGBT pride parade was held in the capital on July 20, cementing a regional leadership role while neighbouring countries turn hostile — the open-environment evidence for visitors.

News reporting (July 2019): an estimated 3,000 people joined the Pride march in the capital on July 12 — six times the turnout of the 2017 first parade; the country's leader publicly backed the event. Quantified growth of visible acceptance.

Blind drops city and organisation names.

rewrites.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised, but in late 2024 the country saw a wave of violence: social-media influencers exhorted followers to 'hunt' gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in the largest city (Abidjan).
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Reputation and regional context: long considered the region's tolerant outlier, the country's standing is now in sharp downshift. A regional rights framework exists — a continental resolution marking a decade of advancing LGBT+ rights — though its protective operation here is not evidenced in this record.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing data: a 2015 academic study of trans-feminine people (travestis) found they face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention, and they have been underserved by the country's rights groups, which distanced themselves. The 2023 official report recorded three community deaths in the year and a transgender man beaten while walking in a suburb of the largest city; it also notes authorities handled complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

This country is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised, but in late 2024 this country saw a wave of violence: social-media influencers exhorted followers to 'hunt' gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in the largest city.
